blocks.html: Part 1: Proving who is calling · Module 2
HMAC request signing
Last reviewed 2026-09-24 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can explain what an HMAC signature proves and what it doesn't, build a correct canonical string, verify a request in the right order, and say when to use asymmetric signatures instead.

Before you start. You should know what a hash is and why a bearer credential like an API key is risky. Module 1 covers API keys.
Published lesson 3 of 27Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: a customer moves 10,000 airline miles into their hotel rewards account. ExampleAir's server sends the transfer to ExampleHotels' API. Company names are fictional.

With a plain API key, the key travels in every request. Anyone who captures one request, from a log, a proxy, or a debugging tool, has the key and can send any request they like. HMAC signing fixes that, but each partial version of it leaves a different attack open:

Attacker has captured one request and tries toAPI keyHMAC onlyHMAC + timestampHMAC + timestamp + nonce
Send a different request with the stolen credentialWorksBlockedBlockedBlocked
Change the amount in the captured requestWorksBlockedBlockedBlocked
Resend it unchanged a week laterWorksWorksBlockedBlocked
Resend it unchanged 10 seconds laterWorksWorksWorksBlocked
Steal the key from the receiver and sign new requestsWorksWorksWorksWorks
The last row never turns green. That's the built-in limit of a shared secret, covered in section 5.
2. Why it works

An HMAC is a hash computed with a secret key mixed in. Only someone holding the key can produce the right value, and anyone holding the key can check it. The sender computes an HMAC over a description of the request and sends the result, the signature, instead of the key.

Three broken assumptions cause most HMAC failures:

  • "A valid signature means a new request." It doesn't. A signature stays valid forever unless the signed data includes something that expires (a timestamp) and something that can only be used once (a nonce).
  • "Both sides will describe the request the same way." Only if they agree on exact bytes. "miles":10000 and "miles": 10000 are the same JSON but different bytes, so they produce different signatures.
  • "The signature proves the sender." It proves the sender holds the key. The receiver holds the same key, so it could have produced the signature too.
3. The control
What gets signed
Both sides build the same canonical string: fixed fields, fixed order, one per line. The body is represented by the SHA-256 hash of its exact bytes.

POST                       method
api.hotel.example          host: blocks replay against another environment
/v2/transfer               path
                           query string (empty here, but always present)
1716307200                 timestamp: limits how long the signature is valid
a1b2c3d4-5678              nonce: makes each request unique
application/json           content type
bb4cc23e...b7a85c78        SHA-256 of the raw body bytes
The right-hand notes are for this page only. They are not part of the string.
How the receiver verifies

1. Look up the key by keyId. Unknown or retired key: reject.
  2. Check the timestamp is within the allowed window of server time. Outside it: reject.
  3. Hash the raw body bytes as received. Never re-serialize parsed JSON, and never trust a hash the caller sent.
  4. Rebuild the canonical string from the received request, compute the HMAC, and compare with a constant-time comparison.
  5. Only then record the nonce, using an atomic "set if absent". Already present: reject. Recording it after the signature check stops forged requests from filling the cache.
  6. Pass the request to authorization and business logic. A valid signature says who sent it, not whether they're allowed to do it.
The whole system
Caller systemsReceiver systemsStored state and secretsRejection path
The setup band and the link check belong to authorization (Part 2). They're shown so you can see where signing stops and authorization starts.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
AlgorithmHMAC-SHA256Your platform or a partner standard mandates another approved hash.
Key32 random bytes per partner, from a secrets managerNever shorter. RFC 2104 strongly discourages keys shorter than the hash output.
Time window5 minutes either side of server timeTighten if clocks are well synchronized and replay is costly. Widen only with a matching nonce TTL.
Nonce storageShared store, entries expire after the windowSkip only if every operation is idempotent by design.
FormatA documented format both sides test againstPrefer RFC 9421 over a custom header when starting fresh. It defines an HMAC-SHA256 option and the canonicalization rules for you.
Symmetric or asymmetricHMAC between two parties who both run their systems wellSwitch to asymmetric signatures if the receiver must not be able to forge, there are many receivers, or you need proof of origin in a dispute.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: the request came from a holder of the key, the signed fields weren't changed, and, with timestamp and nonce checks, it is recent and new.

Doesn't prove: which of the two key holders created it. It doesn't prove the sender is allowed to perform the action. And it proves nothing once the key leaks from either side.

Replay protection is not idempotency. The nonce cache blocks the same request twice. If the caller times out and legitimately retries with a new nonce, the receiver sees a new, valid request. Operations that move money or points also need an idempotency key, such as the caller's transaction ID, stored durably. That's covered in module 11.
6. Prove it

A working implementation must reject every one of these. If any is accepted, the control is broken:

  • A body with one character changed, including added whitespace.
  • The same request sent to a different host or path.
  • A signature made with a different key, or a retired key after the rotation overlap ends.
  • A timestamp outside the window, in either direction.
  • An exact resend inside the window.
  • A valid signature copied onto a request with a different nonce.
Download labs/hmac_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library, and no key is written in it. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3.

$ python3 labs/hmac_lab.py
key source: random, this run only

Part A: integrity. Each attempt uses a fresh verifier.
1. original request              accept
2. one digit changed             reject: bad signature
3. spaces added to JSON          reject: bad signature
4. sent to another host          reject: bad signature
5. signed with the wrong key     reject: bad signature

Part B: freshness and replay. One verifier sees every attempt.
6. first delivery                accept
7. exact replay 10s later        reject: replayed nonce
8. replay 10 minutes later       reject: outside time window
9. new nonce, old signature      reject: bad signature

nonces recorded by the shared verifier: 1

Try next:

  • In Verifier.verify, move the nonce check and the line that records the nonce above the signature check, then run it again. Every verdict stays the same. The last line does not: attempt 9 is forged, and it is now recorded, so the count becomes 2. An attacker who cannot sign can still fill the cache.
  • Remove host from canonical_string. One verdict changes, and only one.
8. Check your understanding

Why is the body hash computed from raw bytes rather than the parsed JSON?

Parsing and re-serializing can change whitespace, key order, or number formatting. The signature covers exact bytes, so the receiver must hash exactly what arrived.

An attacker captures a request and resends it 10 seconds later. Which check stops it?

The nonce check. The timestamp is still inside the window, and the signature is still valid.

ExampleHotels is breached and the shared key leaks. What can the attacker do, and what would have prevented it?

They can sign new requests as ExampleAir, because HMAC gives both sides the same signing power. Asymmetric signatures prevent this: the receiver holds only a public key, which can verify but not sign.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The timestamp still permits a recent request. Recording the nonce after signature verification blocks the exact replay.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. A valid signed request can still be recent. The nonce check is the control that rejects a repeat inside the timestamp window.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardUse HMAC as specified in RFC 2104 and FIPS 198-1, with an approved hash function such as SHA-256.
  • StandardDon't use keys shorter than the hash output length L, which is 32 bytes for SHA-256. RFC 2104 strongly discourages keys shorter than L.
  • StandardCompare signatures with a constant-time function, such as Python's hmac.compare_digest.
  • BaselineSign method, host, path, query, timestamp, nonce, content type, and the SHA-256 of the raw body, in a documented fixed order.
  • BaselineVerify in this order: key lookup, time window, body hash, signature, nonce record. Record the nonce only after the signature verifies.
  • BaselineAccept timestamps within 5 minutes of server time. Keep nonces for at least the same period. Keep clocks synchronized.
  • BaselineStore keys in a secrets manager on both sides, versioned. Rotate with a short overlap in which both versions verify, then retire the old one.
  • BaselineEnsure proxies and gateways pass signed components through unchanged, or verify at the edge.
  • OptionUse RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, with the content-digest field from RFC 9530, instead of a custom format.
  • OptionUse asymmetric signatures when the receiver must not be able to forge caller requests.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• Signed M2M requests cover method, host, path, query, timestamp, nonce, and the raw body hash The canonical format is documented, and both parties test against shared examples.
  • The receiver hashes the raw body bytes it received It never re-serializes parsed JSON, and never trusts a caller-supplied hash.
  • Timestamps are bounded and nonces are rejected on reuse The nonce is recorded only after the signature verifies. The cache TTL is at least the time window.
  • Signatures are compared in constant time Use a library function built for this, not string equality.
  • Keys are per partner, at least 32 bytes, and rotated with an overlap Both sides store keys in a secrets manager. Retired keys are rejected after the overlap ends.
  • Intermediaries do not alter signed components Gateway and proxy behavior is tested with signed requests end to end.
  • The shared-secret limitation is accepted in the threat model Otherwise use asymmetric request signatures.
Sources

• RFC 2104: HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication
  • NIST FIPS 198-1: The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
  • RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures
  • RFC 9530: Digest Fields
  • Python documentation: hmac module

<title>Architecture of an HMAC-signed points transfer</title>
<desc>Setup band: customer links accounts through hotel sign-in, creating a link record, and both companies store the shared secret. Per-request band: the customer app calls the partner transfer service, which signs with a key from its secrets manager and sends over HTTPS to the hotel API gateway, verifier, transfer service, and points ledger. The verifier uses the hotel secrets manager and replay cache; the transfer service uses an idempotency store; the ledger writes an audit log. Failed checks go to a reject box.</desc>

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
AlgorithmHMAC-SHA256Your platform or a partner standard mandates another approved hash.
Key32 random bytes per partner, from a secrets managerNever shorter. RFC 2104 strongly discourages keys shorter than the hash output.
Time window5 minutes either side of server timeTighten if clocks are well synchronized and replay is costly. Widen only with a matching nonce TTL.
Nonce storageShared store, entries expire after the windowSkip only if every operation is idempotent by design.
FormatA documented format both sides test againstPrefer RFC 9421 over a custom header when starting fresh. It defines an HMAC-SHA256 option and the canonicalization rules for you.
Symmetric or asymmetricHMAC between two parties who both run their systems wellSwitch to asymmetric signatures if the receiver must not be able to forge, there are many receivers, or you need proof of origin in a dispute.

checks.title: Signed M2M requests cover method, host, path, query, timestamp, nonce, and the raw body hash
checks.detail: The canonical format is documented, and both parties test against shared examples.

checks.title: The receiver hashes the raw body bytes it received
checks.detail: It never re-serializes parsed JSON, and never trusts a caller-supplied hash.

checks.title: Timestamps are bounded and nonces are rejected on reuse
checks.detail: The nonce is recorded only after the signature verifies. The cache TTL is at least the time window.

checks.title: Signatures are compared in constant time
checks.detail: Use a library function built for this, not string equality.

checks.title: Keys are per partner, at least 32 bytes, and rotated with an overlap
checks.detail: Both sides store keys in a secrets manager. Retired keys are rejected after the overlap ends.

checks.title: Intermediaries do not alter signed components
checks.detail: Gateway and proxy behavior is tested with signed requests end to end.

checks.title: The shared-secret limitation is accepted in the threat model

quiz.summary: Why is the body hash computed from raw bytes rather than the parsed JSON?
quiz.html:
Why is the body hash computed from raw bytes rather than the parsed JSON?

Parsing and re-serializing can change whitespace, key order, or number formatting. The signature covers exact bytes, so the receiver must hash exactly what arrived.

quiz.summary: An attacker captures a request and resends it 10 seconds later. Which check stops it?
quiz.html:
An attacker captures a request and resends it 10 seconds later. Which check stops it?

The nonce check. The timestamp is still inside the window, and the signature is still valid.

quiz.summary: ExampleHotels is breached and the shared key leaks. What can the attacker do, and what would have prevented it?
quiz.html:
ExampleHotels is breached and the shared key leaks. What can the attacker do, and what would have prevented it?

They can sign new requests as ExampleAir, because HMAC gives both sides the same signing power. Asymmetric signatures prevent this: the receiver holds only a public key, which can verify but not sign.
